query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small concentration of lightweight, high-melting-point elements such as titanium (Ti) into a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) will improve its high-temperature mechanical capability by promoting solid-solution strengthening and reducing density, while preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) composed of elements such as Nb, Mo, Ta, and W.
generation.intervention: Add a small concentration (e.g., 5-10 atomic percent) of titanium (Ti) to the RHEA composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing at temperatures exceeding 1000°C under tensile or creep loading, and room-temperature mechanical testing for baseline comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: Solid-solution strengthening and reduced atomic mass of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Titanium, being a lightweight and high-melting-point element, will reduce the overall density of the alloy while contributing to solid-solution strengthening due to its atomic size mismatch with the other refractory elements. This mismatch will impede dislocation motion at high temperatures, enhancing mechanical strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified RHEA will exhibit improved high-temperature mechanical strength (e.g., higher yield strength or creep resistance) compared to the baseline RHEA without Ti, while maintaining comparable room-temperature mechanical properties and achieving a lower density.
generation.baseline: The original RHEA without titanium, tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for Ti concentrations up to 10 atomic percent. Beyond this, phase stability or other properties may be adversely affected.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in high-temperature mechanical properties and the extent of density reduction are uncertain without experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two RHEA samples: one with the baseline composition and one with 5-10 atomic percent Ti added. Perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests at temperatures above 1000°C, and measure room-temperature mechanical properties and density.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified RHEA does not show improved high-temperature mechanical strength or creep resistance compared to the baseline RHEA, or if the room-temperature performance is significantly degraded, the hypothesis will be falsified.
